implementation_notes: The JDK ships the channel: SubmissionPublisher implements Flow.Publisher and delivers every submitted item to each current subscriber, each with its own independent buffer, so the classic registry is replaced by subscribe() and onNext(). submit() blocks when a subscriber's buffer saturates while offer() applies a drop policy, which makes the overflow contract explicit. Choose it for in-process fan-out; use the JMS topic variant when subscribers live in other processes or must survive restarts.
pitfalls: A subscriber that never calls request(n) on its Flow.Subscription receives nothing; ignoring the subscription makes the channel look broken.
Each subscriber has an independent buffer, so one stalled consumer accumulates heap up to maxBufferCapacity before submit() blocks or offer() drops.
Subscriber exceptions cancel that subscription; without the constructor drop/exception handler the failure is easy to miss.

variants.name: Jakarta Messaging topic (brokered fan-out)
variants.implementation_notes: The canonical EIP realization: publish to a topic with a TopicPublisher or MessageProducer, and each TopicSubscriber receives its own copy, where each copy is acknowledged separately and a durable subscription retains messages published while the consumer is offline. Choose it when subscribers live in other processes, need durability across restarts, or must be decoupled by a broker; prefer the JDK publisher for in-process fan-out with no infrastructure.
pitfalls: A non-durable TopicSubscriber receives only messages published while it is active; anything sent during downtime is gone.
Every subscription keeps its own copy and acknowledgement state, so a topic multiplies delivery and storage work by the number of subscribers.
NoLocal must be set when a connection both publishes and subscribes, or a subscriber receives the messages it published itself.
